# Nigrodhamigajātaka (Ja 12)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Nigrodhamigajātaka* (Ja 12), translated in English as *The Banyan Deer*, is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional introductory narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha recounted the story while residing at Jetavana with reference to the mother of the elder Kumāra Kassapa [SuttaCentral; Readings from the Jatakas]. The story is also mentioned in the *Kumārakassapatthera-apadāna* (Tha-Ap 537) [SuttaCentral].
In the core birth story (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta is born as a radiant golden deer and king of a herd, alongside a rival herd led by the future Devadatta [Appleton; Ohnuma 2007]. When both herds are confined to the pleasure grounds of the king of Benares to supply daily venison for the royal table, the two herd leaders agree that one deer selected by lot will present itself each day to prevent widespread slaughter and panic [Appleton; Ohnuma 2007]. When the lot falls upon a pregnant doe, the Bodhisatta intervenes and offers his own life in her place [Spink 2007; Ohnuma 2007]. Awestruck by this extraordinary act of altruistic self-sacrifice and compassion, the king renounces hunting, gives up eating venison, and extends royal immunity (*abhayadāna*) to the Bodhisatta and all other animals [Spink 2007; Appleton; Ohnuma 2007]. In the story's conclusion, the king of Benares is identified as an earlier incarnation of Ānanda and the Bodhisatta as the banyan deer king [Appleton; Readings from the Jatakas].
This Jātaka serves within Buddhist tradition and Indian pilgrim accounts (notably that of Xuanzang) as an etiological legend explaining the origin and name of the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāya*, *Ṛṣipatana*) at Sarnath near Varanasi [Spink 2007; Valisinha 1948; Dhammajoti 1995]. The story is represented visually in Indian and Tibetan Buddhist art, including the wall paintings of Cave 17 at Ajanta and Tibetan narrative thangkas [Spink 2007; Schwartzberg].
According to SuttaCentral, Ja 12 shares a passage-level parallel with the Pali *Nigrodhajātaka* (Ja 445), and has resembling parallels in the Lokottaravādin *Mahāvastu* (*The History of the Deer Park*, Mvu 33), the *Khaggavisāṇa Sutta* (Snp 1.3), and the Gāndhārī *Rhinoceros Sūtra* (GF 5B) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identified no significant Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language matches with a score of 10 or higher [DharmaNexus].
